expectations_used.clarify: Pins the contract down before typing — asks what happens when two bounded segments tie for the longest, and whether a limit of 0 means an empty list rather than one element — instead of assuming every input has a non-empty answer.
expectations_used.approach: States the mechanism aloud before typing it: walk a right edge along values, keep a running count per distinct value, and advance the left edge only while the value just added occurs more than limit times — not merely 'I'll use a hashmap and two pointers'.
expectations_used.communicate: Keeps a running account while the window code is being written — naming which edge of the segment is moving and why the left edge advances when a value exceeds the limit — rather than going quiet through the implementation and explaining only once the suite is green.
expectations_used.implement: Advances the left edge in a loop that decrements the outgoing value's count before moving on, and records the best segment's start index with a strict length comparison so the earlier of two tied segments survives.
expectations_used.verify: Re-runs the suite after each change and hand-traces the scan over [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] with limit 2 to confirm the earlier length-4 bounded segment comes back, rather than stopping at the first green core-path test.
expectations_used.reflect: Explains why a single pass over values is O(n) time and O(k) space in the number of distinct values, and why every slice of a bounded segment is itself bounded — not just restating that the suite passes.

summary: The candidate spent the first several minutes trying to treat this build-from-scratch round as a bug hunt, repeatedly asking for a file or line despite correction, before settling on a sliding-window approach with minimal stated mechanism. Implementation was compressed into a few edits that went straight to 11/11 passing, but with almost no narration during the core coding, and verification consisted of a single test run followed by a request for a score rather than self-driven checking; a solid explanation of the tie-break and complexity only emerged when the interviewer pressed for it.

dimensions.analysis: The candidate did not engage with the actual ambiguity in the spec (tie-break rule, limit=0 edge case) but instead repeatedly asked the interviewer to just locate a bug or hand them a line, even after being told twice this was a build-from-scratch round. This is asking questions, but not the kind that resolve genuine spec ambiguity - it reflects confusion about the round type rather than engagement with the problem's edge cases.

After several unproductive detours, the candidate stated only a generic technique name (sliding window with a counter) without describing the actual mechanism - specifically how and when the left pointer would advance relative to the limit check. This falls short of naming a mechanism specific enough to be wrong.

Aside from brief one-line announcements before writing code (sliding window, setting up counts, dry running example two), there is no narration through the actual implementation window between +332s and +448s where the core logic was written and saved multiple times. The transcript does not explain the path taken to get from an empty file to 11/11 passing.

The edits were scoped and converged quickly to a fully passing suite in a single implementation burst, suggesting a coherent single-pass sliding-window implementation was written directly rather than through visible thrashing. However, since there's no narration accompanying the edits, it's hard to credit sophistication beyond 'it worked'.

The candidate ran the full suite once after implementing and got 11/11, then immediately pivoted to asking for a score rather than tracing any specific case (e.g. the tie-break example) themselves before or after declaring done; the trace of example two they claim to have done at +332s occurred before code existed, and the post-hoc explanation at +552s was only prompted by the interviewer refusing to grade them, not self-initiated verification.

When pushed by the interviewer to justify the fix beyond the green suite, the candidate correctly explained the strict-inequality tie-break mechanism and gave accurate complexity bounds, showing real understanding of why the solution works, though this explanation only came after being explicitly prompted rather than volunteered.
